overview: This two-page Department of State “List of Papers” indexes correspondence between the Japanese Embassy, the Department of State, and the Department of Commerce concerning Japanese merchant-vessel tonnage measurement. The listed papers cover Japan’s 1932 ship-measurement law, 1936 amendments to Articles 21 and 29 of its measurement regulations, and the two governments’ wish to continue reciprocal recognition of tonnage or admeasurement certificates. Later entries record American technical comments and the transmission to Japan of Department of Commerce Circular Letter No. 124 on tonnage openings and the scupperage of shelter-deck space.

subfiles.title: List of papers on the admeasurement of Japanese merchant vessels
subfiles.about: An index summarizes 1933 and 1937 correspondence about Japanese ship-measurement legislation and reciprocal recognition of vessel-tonnage certificates.
subfiles.summary: The first page records an April 15, 1933 Japanese Embassy communication enclosing English translations of a new ship-measurement law and its regulations, effective June 20, 1932, and requesting continued reciprocal recognition of measurement certificates. The continuation records referrals and acknowledgments involving the Departments of State and Commerce. It also indexes 1937 correspondence concerning Japanese Ordinance No. 51 of October 13, 1936, which amended Articles 21 and 29 of the tonnage-measurement regulations, as well as American comments and Circular Letter No. 124 on tonnage openings and shelter-deck scupperage. The United States ultimately concurred in continuing reciprocal recognition of Japanese and American admeasurement certificates.

interest: The file is useful as a compact roadmap to otherwise separate diplomatic and technical exchanges about maritime regulation. It documents how routine matters of naval architecture and customs administration were handled through formal reciprocity between Japan and the United States in the 1930s. Particularly valuable are the references to the effective date of Japan’s 1932 law, the 1936 regulatory amendments, and the American circular on shelter-deck measurement, which allow historians to trace the technical standards underlying international shipping administration.
